data.title: Zámčisko above Modra – a Slavic refuge hillfort in the Lesser Carpathians
data.excerpt: On a mountain promontory above Modra, in the Lesser Carpathians, lies Zámčisko – a hillfort in the shape of a regular horseshoe 115 m long and 105 m wide, which in the time of Great Moravia most probably served as a refuge for the people of the surrounding settlements. Its ramparts were built in two to three phases, the latest of them in the second half of the 13th century, when the fortified area served as a camp and a strongpoint of a military garrison.
data.metaTitle: Zámčisko above Modra – a Slavic refuge hillfort
data.metaDescription: A horseshoe-shaped hillfort above Modra in the Lesser Carpathians: a Great Moravian place of refuge whose ramparts were rebuilt in two to three phases.

keyFacts.label: Shape and dimensions of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: A regular horseshoe measuring 115 x 105 m

keyFacts.label: Length of the ramparts
keyFacts.value: The main rampart a-b-c-d-e measures 280 m, rampart f-b a further 110 m

keyFacts.label: Strategic position
keyFacts.value: The view from the hillfort allowed control of the Pezinok – Častá route over a distance of 15–20 km

keyFacts.label: Building phases of the fortification
keyFacts.value: The rampart fortification was built in two to three separate building phases

keyFacts.label: Investigation of the site
keyFacts.value: The site was first mapped and described by Š. Janšák; in 1999 a trial excavation by Z. Farkaš (Archaeological Museum of the SNM) followed.

keyFacts.label: Metal-detector finds
keyFacts.value: By the end of 2007 a total of 196 metal, almost exclusively iron objects had been collected

keyFacts.label: Military equipment
keyFacts.value: The finds include three arrowheads, spurs with a goad as well as with a rowel, and remains of weapons

keyFacts.label: The legend of Červený Kameň
keyFacts.value: According to legend, the castle of Červený Kameň was originally to have been built at Zámčisko

timeline.description: The phase is dated by finds of two iron ploughshares, a plough coulter, a spearhead and a large knife from the period of the rise and the demise of Great Moravia.

children.text: Zámčisko – Modra

The position of Modra on the southern foot of the Lesser Carpathians determined its origin, its settlement character and the way its inhabitants made a living. We do not know the exact date of Modra's foundation. The beginnings of the possible settlement predecessor of Modra fall in the 9th century, in the heyday of Great Moravia. The Slavic inhabitants of the hamlet (or hamlets) in the north-eastern outer part of today's Ľ. Štúr Square buried their dead in a cemetery in the locality of the so-called Sodoma vineyard.

blocks.caption: Artist's impression of the appearance of the hillfort by Mgr. art. Tomáš Polonský
blocks.alt: Artist's impression of the appearance of the hillfort by Mgr. art. Tomáš Polonský

children.text: Slovak archaeology, however, has so far not given Modra the attention it would deserve, especially since finds were made here by chance in the past which could have marked the beginning of a large-scale archaeological excavation. In 1937 the remains of 9th-century graves were found by chance in Mr Sodoma's vineyard. On his plot of land in Modra Mr Sodoma found several broken graves with skeletons and various objects, and he took the objects to the Slovak Museum in Bratislava. Three years later the find was briefly described by the museum's specialist Dr Ľudmila Kraskovská in the proceedings of the Slovak Museum Society: “In 1937 the Slovak Museum received two pots and a knife from a cemetery of the hillfort period, discovered in Mr Sodoma's vineyard in Modra.” In the following lines she describes the iron knife that was found and two clay vessels of the 9th century decorated with multiple wavy lines.

Mr Sodoma's vineyard was forgotten until 2001, when the plot was located again with great difficulty – and many more years may pass before any excavation takes place here. From Mr Sodoma's find of 1937 it is clear, however, that Modra already existed here at least in the 9th century; to this day, though, we do not know how extensive the occupation here was, nor what relationship this occupation had to the nearby Old Slavic hillfort at Zámčisko.

The area of the hillfort was already in use around 700 BC (i.e. at the time of the greatest flowering of the Molpír hillfort at Smolenice) by the people of the Kalenderberg culture. It was built into the form whose remains can still be seen today (above all the clearly visible defensive ramparts) only in the time of Great Moravia, when the hillfort most probably served as a refuge for the inhabitants of the area of present-day Modra and its surroundings. The original “people of Modra” thus used the hillfort as a place of refuge from the enemy in troubled times. Whenever there was a danger that an enemy would break into the territory of their settlements, the inhabitants took shelter in the fortified Zámčisko, where they had a far better chance of defence than in the unfortified settlement on the site of Modra. After the enemy had left, they returned to their homes again. The hillfort was also used after the rise of the Hungarian state. The 13th century, for example, offered a number of historical events in which the Zámčisko above Modra could have found a use – whether the Mongol invasion, the fighting that took place between the Kingdom of Hungary of the time and the last Babenbergs after the Mongol invasion, the period of the wars between Hungary and the Kingdom of Bohemia, or the period at the end of the 13th century, when the territory of the Lesser Carpathian region was swept by the revolt of Duke Opur against the central government. In these periods the hillfort was put to use, as is attested by various archaeological finds of military type such as spurs, remains of weapons, horseshoes, horseshoe nails and three arrowheads. The hillfort came to an end in a fire.

children.text: The site and the surface of the Zámčisko hillfort were surveyed, mapped, described and assessed by Š. Janšák. He gives its position as 34° 57 1/2' east longitude, 48° 21 3/4' north latitude, 2 km as the crow flies north-east of the village of Kráľová. It lies on a mountain promontory. Its advantageous strategic position is shown by the fact that the view from it allowed control of the routes on the Pezinok – Častá stretch over a distance of 15–20 km.
Janšák describes the natural setting and the fortification of the hillfort as follows:

“It lies on a flat ridge, widened in these parts, of one of the spurs of the Lesser Carpathians, skirted on the west and on the east by mountain brooks which join into one precisely at Harmónia… The natural security of the hillfort is given by the fact that easy access along the ridge exists only from the northern side. On the western and eastern sides there are steep slopes, and on the southern side there occurs a vertical rock 10–15 m high, below it again steeply terraced. The artificial defences were adapted to this natural configuration: they are strongest where access is more comfortable, and they are entirely absent where the sharp slope of the rock suffices on its own for protection.

The hillfort has the shape of a completely regular horseshoe 115 m long and 105 m wide, whose area is closed by rampart a b c d e and by the rock a e, and whose surface is divided into two parts by rampart ľ b. Along their whole length and in all their parts the ramparts are combined with a ditch adjoining them on the outer side, which considerably increases the quality of the fortification and at the same time creates a certain kinship in basic features with the hillfort near Sv. Jur. Rampart a b c d e, 280 m long in all, attaches at point a, at spot height 464, to a steep slope; from there it runs northwards, curves in a great arc to the east as far as point c, where it also reaches the highest point on the ground, i.e. spot height 499. There it turns to the south-east, later to the south, descends to spot height 484 and ends at point e.

Rampart a b is fairly flat; on the outer side it rises 2–3 m above the bottom of the adjoining ditch, and towards the interior of the hillfort it barely projects 30–40 cm above the surface. At point c it reaches a height of 7 m above the bottom of the ditch, and from there its height gradually falls to 5 and 4 m, while at point d the ditch is hewn into the rock and the material thus obtained has been used to make the bank. Rampart f b, 110 m long, is far more massive. The difference in height between its crest and the bottom of the adjoining ditch amounts to 5–6 m along almost its entire length. At a distance of about 40 m northwards from rampart b c there occurs a small transverse ridge i j (formed naturally, by an accumulation of rock boulders and timber), which the inhabitants of the hillfort could use to advantage as a first defence against access from the north. The circuit rampart a b c d e is broken through in three places: at points h, b, c. Entrance b appears to be the original one, serving for entry into the hillfort; the position of rampart b), c) makes it possible to block it off. Entrances ch g were established later.

children.text: Zámčisko consists of two enclosures: a b ľ a (T) with an area of 3, 9 a, and f b c d e f (II) with an area of (), I a. Enclosure I occupies a relatively very steep slope of 45%, less suitable for habitation, standing in for the function of a bailey. Enclosure II extends over a flat back sloping gently towards all four cardinal points, both lengthwise and crosswise, which offers the possibility of a longer and more permanent stay. Enclosure I faces entirely, and Enclosure II for the greater part, towards the south, which is also a very favourable circumstance for living conditions. The spring P at the eastern end of rampart i j supplies water through the greater part of the year, even in a wet summer.

children.text: S. Janšák's work was followed up by a trial excavation in 1999, carried out by the Archaeological Museum of the Slovak National Museum in Bratislava at the initiative of the Municipal Office and the state administration in Modra. Under the direction of Z. Farkaš the work concentrated on the investigation of the upper fortification of the hillfort, and two trenches were opened. The first cut through the northern rampart of the upper hillfort, the second sectioned the northern wing of the western gateway of the inner defences. As Z. Farkaš states in his study of the trial excavation at the Zámčisko site, “the sections through the ramparts of the ‘acropolis’ of Zámčisko attested a multi-phase construction, but did not make it possible to resolve its relationship to the bailey.” The relatively modest accompanying material, as well as the objects obtained by “treasure hunters” with the help of detectors, makes it possible above all to date the latest phase of the fortification to the 10th and the beginning of the 11th century; in this fortification a military garrison was stationed “at least occasionally”, housed perhaps in both light and more permanent ground-level dwellings of timber…”
Zdenek Farkaš summarised the most recent results of the archaeological excavations in the edited volume Modra v premenách stáročí (Modra through the Changes of the Centuries) as follows:

The rampart fortification consisted of two to three separate building phases. In the northern part, at the point of easiest access, the earliest fortification probably consisted of two ramparts, most likely of timber-and-earth construction, between which a deep ditch, preserved to this day, was dug in the third building phase. The fortification itself was founded on the original clayey-sandy subsoil, and the original terrain was used in such a way that the outer bank rested with its back against a natural rock. The earliest rampart consists of markedly ashy soil mixed with beech charcoal. It cannot be ruled out that the pronounced ashy layer did not arise during a fire at the hillfort, but during the burning off of the vegetation on the future building site and the subsequent heaping of a mixture of earth and ash into the body of the fortification. The width of the destruction layer of the front rampart, originally probably also the lower one, reached 1.9 m, and that of the inner one 5.6 m.

children.text: So far the hardest to place in time is the
earliest building phase

. A larger fragment of a vessel of the Late Bronze Age was found by an amateur. Despite the donor's assertion, however, it has so far not been possible to prove an unambiguous relationship of the sherd to Zámčisko. Among the finds obtained during the metal-detector survey, a sickle-shaped iron knife belongs to the ancient types,
probably from the Hallstatt period

. According to unverified information, it was precisely bronze objects of the Late Bronze Age and the Hallstatt period that were among the main objects of interest of the metal detectorists. Some of them allegedly also ended up in the private collections of certain inhabitants of Modra. It is precisely making them accessible that could move our knowledge of the town's earliest history a significant step forward.

children.text: In the following (middle) phase

the already destroyed remains of the original inner rampart were levelled and cut through by a foundation trench running parallel to the line of the fortification, the bottom of which reached down to the rocky bedrock. Judging by the continuous layer of burnt beech wood overlying the older fortification in front of the trench, the new wall, with its back resting against a face anchored in the trench, was perhaps built on a timber platform for reasons of stability. Its front part, however, has not survived to this day.

The middle phase of the construction of the fortification is dated above all by 2 iron ploughshares, a plough coulter, a spearhead, a large knife similar to the one found in one of the graves in Mr Sodoma's vineyard, and perhaps also by some other objects of the 9th – early 10th century, that is, the period corresponding to the rise and the demise of
Great Moravia.

Unfortunately, sherds of pottery of this period are so far entirely absent, although they otherwise belong among the most frequent archaeological finds at fortified as well as unfortified settlements. Whether this is connected with the state of research, with the relatively small area uncovered, or merely with the refuge function of Zámčisko in the Great Moravian period will probably only be recognisable through a new, more generous excavation. In any case the existence of the hillfort attests the importance and the density of the occupation of the Modra area during Great Moravia, with its own fortified administrative centre, or at least a place of refuge and a strongpoint for the inhabitants of several smaller hamlets in the vicinity.
The latest

, already the third fortification in the northern part of the hillfort consisted of a grillage construction of oak timber, which also covered the older foundation trench. It included a predominantly stony bank rising right up to the present-day surface. In the last phase of the construction of the fortification, the older (?) ditch between the two original ramparts was dug, or at least substantially deepened. It was cut into the natural quartzite bedrock and the material from it was heaped into both the main and the outer rampart. Of the timber construction of the wall, thin layers of charred wood have survived to this day, and perhaps also the partly differently coloured heaped layers.

Most of the iron finds recorded on the overall plan of the hillfort were nails of various shapes and functions. Apart from numerous “horseshoe nails”, the presence of horses at Zámčisko is also attested by 14 horseshoes or fragments of them. In two cases, however, the horseshoes could have been part of heavy hobnailed footwear. Not all the horseshoes need be connected with the period of the existence of the fortification. After losing its military function, Zámčisko gradually turned into today's wood, and it was used as such, including the felling of timber and its haulage by horse teams. Spurs were part of the rider's equipment, and a relatively chronologically sensitive part at that. Two of them belonged to the types with a goad and two were already fitted with a movable rowel. Among the interesting finds were an iron spit lying directly on a hearth by the western gateway, and a set of three keys, two of them so-called Gothic rotary keys with a flat ward and one a sliding key from a padlock. Military equipment forms a separate category, among it three arrowheads.

children.text: The pottery sherds and the great majority of the iron objects apparently make it possible to place the last building phase of Zámčisko fairly reliably in the second
half of the 13th century

, when the fortified area served as a camp and at the same time as a strongpoint of a military garrison. Unfortunately, the archaeological material currently available does not make it possible to link it unambiguously with any of the military and political events that took place in this territory in the second half of the 13th and the beginning of the 14th century. Most recently J. Žudel does not rule out that the old fortification above Modra was used in the period of the wars of the Kingdom of Hungary with Přemysl Otakar II, and that it was precisely Bohemian troops that could for a time have controlled the adjacent territory from the advantageous position of Zámčisko.

In none of the three building phases was the front or the rear of the wall reinforced with a small stone wall. In the last phase the outer rampart apparently had no internal timber construction and consisted only of a simple bank.

children.text: Insights into the development of the fortification at the so-called western gateway of the acropolis were considerably affected by erosion. Nevertheless it was established that here too the earliest rampart was built on levelled original terrain and that, as in the northern part of the fortification, it again consisted of ashy brownish earth with remains of charred wood, this time, however, with traces of an original internal construction, most likely of the grillage type. Of the first bank, however, only a layer 15 to 35 cm thick has survived to this day. In the younger rampart resting on it only slight traces remained of an internal timber construction that cannot be defined more closely. As in the north, no traces of a possible stone front revetment wall were found here either. Indistinct dark patches above the inner edge of the ditch, perhaps pits originally holding vertical supporting posts, could, however, have been part of the front face.

The absence of any construction and the undisturbed bank of the older rampart body in the gateway do not rule out that the gateway is younger than the ramparts and is therefore not connected with the original fortification. S. Janšák already regarded all the present entrances into the fortification as younger than the line of the wall, with the exception of the passage between the bailey and the main rampart.

Neither in the rampart bank nor in the fill of the ditch was any archaeological material found that would allow the individual building phases to be dated. The extent of the excavation and its focus, in turn, did not allow a larger space to be uncovered inside the enclosed area, in which possible internal buildings could have been traced and which would also have yielded a larger quantity of well datable material. Only 61 fragments of clay vessels come from the archaeological trenches. The imperfect firing of the pottery probably points to the production of village potters. We date this pottery to the middle of the 13th century.

Both archaeological excavations established that Zámčisko was visited more or less regularly by various treasure hunters equipped with metal detectors, who left behind numerous “hunters' holes” on the ground and metal objects of no interest to them hung on the trees or laid down around them. In addition, attempts at larger unprofessional diggings were also recorded, for example at the highest point of the fortification. The archaeologists of the Slovak National Museum – Archaeological Museum in Bratislava therefore undertook a comprehensive survey of the fortified area with metal detectors. By the end of 2007 it was thus possible to assemble a collection of 196 metal, almost exclusively iron objects, coming mostly from the excavation of 1999. A few pieces also reached the collections of the Slovak National Museum as a gift from a local collector. In 2006 the original collection was supplemented by a so far isolated later find of a Gothic key from another collector, to which a small silver coin – the first known from this site – was allegedly corroded; after being taken out of the ground, however, it succumbed entirely to corrosion.
In conclusion I will add an interesting
legend connected with the Zámčisko above Modra:

The castle of Červený Kameň (near Častá/Píla) was in fact supposed to have been built at Zámčisko. The building was even begun, but whatever was built during the day was carried overnight by some unknown force to the place where Červený Kameň now stands. This was perhaps meant as a warning that the castle should be built in a different place.
